plan.summary: Budget should lean on the two home publishers — Northbed (room-finishing add-on) and Hearthstone Goods (gifting and new-home occasions, non-toxic values) — with tests at Studiogrid for the self-care ritual angle and Heartfoot for its explicit gifting mode; everything else is off-moment despite flattering income and price scores.

recommended.name: Northbed
recommended.tier_reason: The score treated this as generic category adjacency, but the record shows a direct purchase-moment link: someone who just spent on bedding/bath is furnishing a room, and a candle is the classic finishing object for that room. Notes explicitly flag 'High cross-sell with home and wellness', and a $38 candle is a fifth of the $164 basket.
recommended.rationale: Design-conscious buyers who just bought bedding or bath textiles are mid-project on a room, and the publisher's own notes claim 'High cross-sell with home and wellness' — a hand-poured soy candle is a cheap, aesthetic finishing add-on to a $164 order.

evidence.quote: High cross-sell with home and wellness

recommended.risk: Reach is modest at 3.6M impressions, so volume will be capped even at a good conversion rate.

recommended.name: Hearthstone Goods
recommended.tier_reason: Tag overlap only saw kitchen≈home_decor, but the notes name the exact occasion this brand sells into: 'Gifting and new-home life events drive purchase.' Candles are the default gift/housewarming add-on, and the 'non_toxic' sensibility matches 'No synthetic fragrances'.
recommended.rationale: Shoppers here are already in gifting or housewarming mode per 'Gifting and new-home life events drive purchase', and a non-toxic-minded kitchen audience maps cleanly onto natural soy wax with no synthetic fragrances at $38 against a $198 basket.

evidence.quote: Gifting and new-home life events drive purchase

recommended.risk: 2.8M impressions is the smallest of the home publishers; gifting-driven traffic may also concentrate seasonally.

test.name: Studiogrid
test.rationale: Users here are booking spa and yoga sessions and are 'actively spending on self-care and fitness', so an at-home relaxation candle at roughly the price of a class ($38 vs $42) is a plausible extension of the ritual — worth measuring whether a service booking converts to a physical-goods purchase at all.

evidence.quote: Users are actively spending on self-care and fitness

test.risk: Booking an appointment is a different mental mode from buying an object; service checkouts often convert poorly to physical product offers, and the gifting angle is absent here.

test.name: Heartfoot
test.tier_reason: The score only counted a weak 'gift' tag match, but this publisher's own subcategories include 'gifting' and the notes report 'Strong gifting season uplift (Nov-Dec)' — the shopper is often already in gift-buying mode, which is the advertiser's primary occasion (gift 1.0).
test.rationale: Socks-as-gifts shoppers are literally in gift mode ('Strong gifting season uplift (Nov-Dec)'), and a $38 hand-poured candle is a natural second gift on a $52 basket; worth testing whether that mode transfers outside apparel.
test.risk: Gift-mode overlap may be seasonal only, and the audience 'responds to social-good messaging' rather than craft/heritage claims, so copy may need reworking.

test_plan.promote_if: CPA at or below the $11.40 target after 14 days: move it to core.
test_plan.cut_if: CPA above the $14.82 maximum, or no conversions after 14 days: stop it.

test_plan.risk: Gift-mode overlap may be seasonal only, and the audience 'responds to social-good messaging' rather than craft/heritage claims, so copy may need reworking.

test_plan.cut_if: CPA above the $14.82 maximum, or no conversions after 14 days: stop it.

launch_summary.summary: $8,500 of the $10,000 budget goes to two home publishers, Northbed and Hearthstone Goods, where shoppers are finishing rooms or buying for gifting and new homes and care about non-toxic materials. The remaining $1,500 splits evenly between two tests: Studiogrid, to see whether a spa or yoga booking carries over into an at-home relaxation purchase, and Heartfoot, to see whether gift mode transfers outside apparel. Each test is judged after 14 days against the $11.40 target cost per new customer.
uncertainties: The $38 first order value is assumed, and both the $11.40 target and $14.82 maximum cost per new customer are built on it.
The 30% allowable ratio stands in for real margin and lifetime value, and assumes one-time purchases rather than repeat or subscription buying.
The ad written for The Affluent Classic won't run because no placement's shoppers fit that persona, so the heritage and craft angle goes largely untested.
